If $x\in\mathbb Z$, then for every $h$ we have $x+h\in\mathbb Z$ if and only if $x-h\in\mathbb Z$, so $f(x+h)=f(x-h)$ and hence $f(x+h)-f(x-h)=0$.
If $x\notin\mathbb Z$, let $d=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb Z)>0$. For $|h|<d$, neither $x+h$ nor $x-h$ is an integer, so again $f(x+h)-f(x-h)=0$. Thus
\[
\lim_{h\to0}\bigl(f(x+h)-f(x-h)\bigr)=0
\]
for every $x\in\mathbb R$.
However, $f$ is not continuous at any integer $n$: $f(n)=1$, while for the sequence $x_k=n+1/(k+\sqrt2)$, which consists of nonintegers and converges to $n$, we have $f(x_k)=0$. Therefore $f$ need not be continuous.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Consider the function
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x\text{ is an integer},\\0,&x\text{ is not an integer}.
\end{cases}
\]
For an integer $x$, the numbers $x+h$ and $x-h$ are integers simultaneously: this occurs exactly when $h\in\mathbb Z$. Hence $f(x+h)=f(x-h)$ for every $h$.

For a noninteger $x$, there is a nearest integer at a positive distance from $x$. Let $d=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb Z)>0$. If $|h|<d$, both $x+h$ and $x-h$ remain nonintegers. Therefore $f(x+h)=f(x-h)=0$ for all sufficiently small $h$.

Consequently, for every $x\in\mathbb R$,
\[
\lim_{h\to0}\bigl(f(x+h)-f(x-h)\bigr)=0.
\]
Nevertheless, $f$ is discontinuous at every integer $n$, since $f(n)=1$ but $f(y)=0$ for every noninteger $y$ arbitrarily close to $n$. Thus the stated condition does not imply continuity.
\end{proof}
